title: Ryan Batchelor – Clifford Capital Partners (Manager Meetings, EP.11)
summary:

into sustainable wide moat businesses for core holdings and out-of-favor stocks for deep value
holdings. The overlap of interest in moats led WCM to take an equity stake in Clifford three
years ago. We're growth stock managers

thesis: This episode argues that institutional managers at Clifford Capital Partners identify specific undervalued opportunities in retail and consumer sectors, citing GameStop, Abercrombie & Fitch, and American Express as key examples. The thesis relies on fundamental factors such as short-term leases, strong balance sheets, and free cash flow dynamics to justify bullish stances, while also acknowledging past losses at Morning Star and the neutral view on Costco.

claims.claim: The firm believed GameStop was undervalued due to short-term leases with zero-cost exit and an upcoming console cycle, seeing a conservative fair value of $20 a share.
claims.quote: So we believe this was a cyclical downturn for GameStop. And yes, there are secular pressures, but the valuation, the cash flows, the balance sheet were all excellent. claims.claim: Amazon is viewed as a major influence on retail, putting pressure on brick-and-mortar retailers, which creates investment opportunities for the firm.
claims.quote: So, for instance, Amazon.com has had a clear influence on retail across the world, really, but across the country, big time. Brick-and-mortar retailers under severe pressure because of online presence, not just from people moving online, but retailers having to invest in online capabilities, which has hurt their profitability.

claims.claim: The firm identified Abercrombie and Fitch as undervalued due to strong balance sheet, free cash flow exceeding earnings, and an inflection point where e-commerce would overtake revenue decline within 18 to 24 months.
claims.quote: So we valued the company and said, in rough terms, business is trading at half of what Hollister is worth. And in the worst case scenario, we could come up with, how much lower could the stock go. claims.claim: The speaker believes American Express has a fantastic business model with strong economics and inflation protection, and that the Costco loss will unlock capital for share repurchases.
claims.quote: Amex has a fantastic business model. They keep all the economics of their cards, which is rare. And also inflation protection, which is a big deal in today's environment.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Costco grew and could demand better terms, leading to a business decision where Amex walked away from the business.
claims.quote: Costco had grown, obviously could demand better terms, and Amex said we won't play with those terms. They walked away from the business.

claims.claim: The speaker admits that a stock pick at Morning Star was not a good stock due to management improprieties and aspects he had never seen before, leading to significant losses.
claims.quote: There were some management improprieties. There were some aspects of this asset that I had never seen before. The danger is not knowing what you don't know as a young and experienced analyst and the stock was not a good stock.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Seth Klarman as a phenomenal hedge fund manager who compounded net of fees over 30% or something like 25% annually for 20 plus years.
claims.quote: A close second is Seth Clarman, a little less well-known, phenomenal hedge fund manager. Since the mid-80s, at one point, he was compounding net of fees over 30% or something like 25% annually for 20 plus years.
